benefits: One page for both directions, so you never open the wrong converter.
Union of all object keys becomes the header row, so ragged JSON still converts cleanly.
Nested objects and arrays are safely stringified into their cells instead of breaking.
Everything runs locally; API keys or private rows in your data are never transmitted.

faqs.a: Both a single object and an array of objects are accepted. A single object becomes a one-row CSV; an array becomes one row per object.
faqs.q: Does the JSON have to be an array?

faqs.a: All keys from all objects are collected, in first-seen order. Objects missing a key get an empty cell in that column.
faqs.q: What if my objects have different keys?

faqs.a: They are converted with JSON.stringify into the cell, so the information is preserved as compact JSON text inside the CSV field.
faqs.q: How are nested objects handled in JSON to CSV?

faqs.a: The first CSV row becomes the property names. Turn to CSV to JSON mode, paste, and you get an array of objects with optional pretty printing.
faqs.q: How do I go from CSV back to JSON?

faqs.a: The converter reads the JSON you pasted and shows a clear error message pointing at invalid JSON. Fix the syntax, for example a missing comma or quote, and it converts.

json-to-csv.formula: CSV row = join(values in header order, delimiter)  |  JSON object = { header: cell } per row
howTo: Pick a direction: JSON to CSV or CSV to JSON.
Paste your data into the box, or press Sample.
Choose the CSV delimiter: comma, semicolon, tab or pipe.
For CSV to JSON, toggle pretty printing if you want indented output.
Press Download to save the file, or Copy to paste it into your code.
keyFacts: Converts JSON to CSV and CSV to JSON on one page with a direction toggle.
JSON keys become the CSV header row in first-seen order.
Nested values are stringified into their cells instead of being dropped.
CSV parsing handles quoted fields, escaped quotes and line breaks.
Invalid JSON shows a friendly error instead of crashing.

limitations: Flat tables only; nested structures are stringified, not expanded.
Duplicate JSON keys keep the last value, as per JSON rules.
Very large inputs (tens of MB) can make the browser tab sluggish.
CSV headers are treated as plain text property names.

json-to-csv.workedExample:
JSON to CSV input:
[{"name":"Aarav Sharma","age":25},{"name":"Priya Verma","age":30}]

Output CSV:
name,age
Aarav Sharma,25
Priya Verma,30

2 records, 2 fields each.

CSV to JSON input:
name,age
Aarav Sharma,25

Pretty output:
[
  { "name": "Aarav Sharma", "age": "25" }
]

Note: CSV values stay strings in this direction.
